quote: Es sei etwa $x = \alpha$ eine Nullstelle von $R$ dann handelt es sich um die Frage: wie
english: Let, say, x = α be a zero of R; then the question is: how
topic: An algebraic proof of the existence of algebraic functions for a given Riemann surface, beginning with an equation in y with polynomial coefficients, its discriminant, and a substitution z to obtain a new equation whose discriminant factors as R^2 d.

triage.modern_statement: The sentence breaks off after 'how', so its exact question can't be pinned down. From the context, it most likely concerns this setup: an algebraic function field is given by F(x,y)=0, and a transformed equation in z has discriminant D(x)=R(x)^2·d(x). Hilbert seems to ask how the factor R behaves at a root x=α. In modern terms: is (x−α) an 'inessential' discriminant divisor, i.e. one that comes only from singularities of the chosen plane model (the index of Z[x][z] in the integral closure) and not from real branching of the Riemann surface? The related task is to show it can be removed by choosing another primitive element z, or to describe the branches/places over α (Puiseux expansions, local integral basis). This is the classical split of the discriminant into an index part and the field discriminant.
triage.answered_by: If the reading above is right, the issue was already handled in the classical algebraic theory of algebraic functions: Dedekind & Weber (Crelle 92, 1882), Kronecker's work on inessential discriminant divisors, and Hensel & Landsberg (Theorie der algebraischen Funktionen einer Variablen, 1902). No source names this specific note or says what Hilbert did with it.

evidence.claim: Dedekind and Weber published 'Theorie der algebraischen Functionen einer Veränderlichen' in J. reine angew. Math. 92 (1882), 181–290, the founding purely algebraic treatment of algebraic functions and Riemann surfaces.
Dedekind and Kronecker both studied inessential (common) discriminant divisors, which arise when the discriminant of a generating polynomial has factors beyond the field discriminant.
Hensel and Landsberg published 'Theorie der algebraischen Funktionen einer Variablen' (1902), a standard algebraic/arithmetic treatment of algebraic functions.

triage.why: The note stops mid-sentence ('wie' = 'how') with no actual question, so it can't be identified for certain. The surrounding page (discriminant splitting as R^2·d after a substitution z) points to the standard question of how the extra square factor R behaves at its roots, as opposed to real branch points. That was settled by the 1880s–1900s algebraic theory of Kronecker, Dedekind–Weber and Hensel–Landsberg, and today it is routine (integral bases, normalization). It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The sources found don't mention this note.
